title: What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills · hancrafted
description: When a task you keep explaining should become a skill, how to write its description as the moment you'd need it, what goes into the skill and what stays in project context, and what a shared skill needs to stay right: an owner, a version, tests and a retirement date.

The description (1/3) Page 1 of 3 The description is the trigger The AI sees only the name and description up front, and the description decides when the skill loads. We've reached a new site. loaded: name and description loaded at startup: name, description Skill index · the manual's index front matter of each SKILL.md Samples name: samples Samples. Collect sediment sample name: collect-sediment-sample Take a sediment sample at a new site Misc. procedures name: misc-procedures Various procedures. Run camera survey name: run-camera-survey Film a strip of seabed behind it, every card: not loaded yet body: not loaded yet Two descriptions for the same skill. Which one would you open? Vague description stays shut “Samples” collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Samples. --- Clear description lit by today's task “Take a sediment sample at a new site” collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Take a sediment sample at a new site. --- Did you know? Information scent : the cue on a label that tells you whether it leads where you want to go. Pirolli and Card, Xerox PARC, 1999: a finding about people searching. Borrowing it for the AI is an inference. In the story: From the pilot's chair: the index is open, every card behind it closed. “If the description doesn't convey when the skill is useful, the agent won't know to reach for it.” At startup the agent reads only name and description from each SKILL.md ; the body stays closed.

Your request, on the day of the dive “Grab some mud here before we move on.” Your prompt to the coding agent > Grab some mud here before we move on. by meaning: mud → seabed, here → new site Skill index Two descriptions for the same skill; the AI sees only these lines. Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed . Not for water samples or filming. --- The “not for” line is optional: only Google's guide recommends it 2 Second step: write its description as the moment you'd need it. A description says what the skill does and when to use it; Claude chooses among potentially 100+ skills by it The standard: a description “Should describe both what the skill does and when to use it”; Anthropic adds specific triggers and contexts

The description (3/3) Page 3 of 3 More skills, harder choice Skills that look alike leave the AI guessing; a short list in the project instructions takes the guess away. Skill index: 8 skills, each by name and description .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md name + description Sample sample Collect water sample collect-water-sample Take sample take-sample Collect sediment sample collect-sediment-sample Film a transect film-transect Seabed sample v2 seabed-sample-v2 Log the dive log-dive Collect mud sample collect-mud-sample Project instructions In this project, use these three skills: # AGENTS.md ## Skills In this project, use these three skills: 1 Collect sediment sample - collect-sediment-sample 2 Film a transect - film-transect 3 Log the dive - log-dive Project instructions, always loaded AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md 1 Skill index the manual's index name and description of every skill Near-twins sound alike, so the AI has to guess between them. .claude/skills/ sample/SKILL.md take-sample/SKILL.md seabed-sample-v2/ collect-mud-sample/SKILL.md … 8 in all 2 Project instructions the project brief on the wall always loaded; CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md elsewhere A short list there says which three skills to use, so there is no crowded choice. # AGENTS.md ## Skills In this project, use these three skills: - collect-sediment-sample - film-transect - log-dive Hick's law, a finding about people People take longer to choose as the information in the choice grows. Hick 1952, Hyman 1953: choice-reaction experiments in people. That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result. Vercel's agent evals: pass rate The skill, by default 53 % + a line in AGENTS.md telling the agent to use its skill 79 % With the line, the skill was opened in 95%+ of cases. One docs skill, one framework. A docs index replacing the skill reached 100%. Name it as an action, lowercase words joined by hyphens Anthropic 's skill-authoring best practices: names use lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only; action-oriented names such as process-pdfs and analyze-spreadsheets are listed as acceptable (the gerund, processing-pdfs , is preferred), and patterns should stay consistent across a collection. collect-sediment-sample film-transect log-dive In the story: Near-twin cards leave the pilot guessing; the list on the wall settles it.

That is the loan: you get the speed now. Five minutes, from a good run. That is the loan: you get the speed now. --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- Project details changed Weeks later the site list changed The skill still names last season's sites. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md, step 1 1. Check the site on the site list. (the list is last season's) A new tool arrived Months later a new robot arm Step 3 still describes the old arm. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md, step 3 Run scripts/arm-preset.py (written for the old arm) A description now overlaps another skill's Later still an index line overlaps another card “Collect sediment sample” and “Seabed survey” now sound alike, so the AI can reach for the wrong one. two descriptions the agent chooses between collect-sediment-sample: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. seabed-survey: Use when we reach a new site and need to survey the seabed. Next fix · … and counting One skill, over months sites arm overlap next writing five minutes keeping it right one block per fix An illustration, not a measurement. Technical debt “Shipping first time code is like going into debt.” The interest: “every minute spent on not-quite-right code”. Ward Cunningham, 1992, about software. The parallel to skills is ours. Writing thirty skills is easy. Owning thirty is the hard part. In the story: A card with a running tag, like a loan statement.

Keeping it alive (2/4) Page 2 of 4 The model changes, the skill doesn't A model update changes who reads your skill, so a skill that worked yesterday can behave differently today. The skill, unchanged collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md same words Collect sediment sample Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- … 2. Descend slowly to the seabed. Model update Your provider ships a new version of the model. The skill keeps the same words, and the same instruction now gives a different result. The same collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md , a new model version reading it. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md unchanged model new version today: stops short yesterday Different model or agent A colleague runs your skill in another app or agent, even on the same model, and it reads the same words its own way. The same collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md , run in Claude Code and in Codex: another agent, even on the same model. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md unchanged agent, model another one today: into the silt yesterday Did you know? Lehman's laws Software in use must keep being adapted, or it becomes progressively less satisfactory. Here the skill stays put and the world around it moves. Disputed: of the laws, only continuing change and continuing growth held in every study reviewed. Same words, a new reader Anthropic's prompting guide has model-specific sections on where "a single model behaves differently"; OpenAI notes that prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work". Your SKILL.md is read as text by whichever model runs it. Anthropic's guide shows "what to change in your prompt" per model; OpenAI: prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work". In the story: Same card, two dives, two depths. Analogy only: the pilot keeps his piloting and forgets the days. A skill file is read as text, closer to a written note than to a trained skill.

A thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

An AI model that forgets every morning Each AI conversation starts fresh: Mollick's forgetful coworker Ethan Mollick advises treating AI "like an infinitely patient new coworker who forgets everything you tell them each new conversation" 1 . Claude Code sessions each begin "with a fresh context window" and only written files carry knowledge across 2 . "Amnesiac" is the Episode's word, not Mollick's. Sources (2) Ethan Mollick, Getting started with AI: Good enough prompting, One Useful Thing (24 Nov 2024) ( opens in a new tab ) oneusefulthing.org Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com

A skill hands the AI your procedure A skill spares you the repeat Anthropic contrasts skills with prompts: a skill spares you from repeating the same guidance across conversations 1 . When a request matches a skill's description, Claude reads SKILL.md and only then does that content enter the context 1 . Calling a skill by name loads it too, as the Slide on two ways to call a skill shows. Sources (1) Anthropic, Agent Skills overview ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

The description No speaker notes for this Slide.

The description is the trigger Description carries the whole burden because only name and description load at startup, "the description carries the entire burden of triggering. If the description doesn't convey when the skill is useful, the agent won't know to reach for it" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Descriptions and information scent Pirolli and Card's abstract names "information scent models, which address the identification of information value from proximal cues" 1 . It is a finding about people foraging for information; that a vague label gives a model less to go on is an inference, not their finding. The page-646 definition was read second-hand. Sources (1) Pirolli and Card, Information Foraging (Psychological Review, 1999) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

Name the trigger, not the content A description says what and when the standard says a description "Should describe both what the skill does and when to use it" and include keywords that help agents identify relevant tasks 1 . Anthropic adds specific triggers and contexts, because Claude chooses among potentially 100+ skills by it 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Write the description in the user's words "Use imperative phrasing", "Focus on user intent, not implementation", and "Err on the side of being pushy. Explicitly list contexts where the skill applies" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io "Not for" lines in a description: Google's advice alone the standard and Anthropic recommend no "not for" clause in a description. Over-triggering is handled there by testing near-miss queries that share keywords but need something different, which "test whether the description is precise, not just broad" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io The "not for" clause in Google's Day 3 Google's Day 3 whitepaper writes "explicitly state what it is not for", gives the example "Do NOT use for employee shift scheduling or financial accounting", and its checklist says "Include when NOT to use to prevent over-triggering" 1 . It calls the description "your routing algorithm. It is the only thing the model sees to decide whether to load the Agent Skill" and asks to "be pushy if the model under-triggers". It gives no measurement that the clause helps, so it is Google's vendor guidance, a choice between sources. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com

More skills, harder choice Choosing among many skills: Hick and Hyman, a finding about people Hick applied information theory to choice-reaction-time experiments with up to ten alternatives 1 . Hyman reports that reaction time rises linearly with the amount of information in the choice 2 . That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result. Sources (2) Hick, On the Rate of Gain of Information (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1952) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Hyman, Stimulus Information as a Determinant of Reaction Time (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1953) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org An AGENTS.md index beat skills: Vercel's test a line in AGENTS.md telling the agent to use its skill raised the pass rate from 53% to 79%, and the skill was opened in 95% or more of cases 1 . A compressed docs index of about 8KB in AGENTS.md, replacing the skill, reached 100%. Vercel's working theory: no decision point, and skills load only when invoked 1 . It is one docs skill for one framework, not a procedure. Sources (1) Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com Skills too broad or too narrow the standard warns that skills "scoped too broadly become hard to activate precisely", while too narrow forces several to load 1 . No source measures lookalike skills lowering the pick rate directly. Sources (1) Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Name each skill as an action Anthropic's skill-authoring best practices say a skill's name uses lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only, prefer the gerund form (processing-pdfs) and list action-oriented names such as process-pdfs and analyze-spreadsheets as an acceptable alternative; they advise against inconsistent patterns within a skill collection 1 . This Episode names its skills in the action form, collect-sediment-sample. Sources (1) Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

Every skill is a loan Skill upkeep as technical debt: Cunningham's words "Shipping first time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite." "Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest on that debt." 1 He names the failure mode as "the failure to consolidate". The software parallel to skills is an inference, not his claim. Sources (1) Cunningham, The WyCash Portfolio Management System ( opens in a new tab ) c2.com

The model changes, the skill doesn't Skills in a changing world: Lehman's first two laws, and their limits "E-type systems must be continually adapted else they become progressively less satisfactory"; complexity increases "unless work is done to maintain or reduce it" 1 . The laws are disputed: only continuing change and continuing growth were validated by all studies reviewed 2 , and Linux grew super-linearly 3 . Sources (3) Lehman, Ramil and Wernick, Metrics and Laws of Software Evolution: The Nineties View ( opens in a new tab ) users.ece.utexas.edu Herraiz, Rodriguez, Robles and Gonzalez-Barahona, The evolution of the laws of software evolution: a discussion based on a systematic literature review ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Godfrey and Tu, Evolution in Open Source Software: A Case Study ( opens in a new tab ) plg2.cs.uwaterloo.ca Each model reads the same instructions differently Anthropic's guide has model-specific sections on where "a single model behaves differently and what to change in your prompt" 1 ; OpenAI notes that prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work" 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Prompting best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com OpenAI, GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide ( opens in a new tab ) developers.openai.com The model's memory and patient H.M.: an analogy that breaks at the skill H.M. learned mirror drawing and kept it across 3 days while remembering none of the sessions 1 , because skills are stored by a memory system outside the damaged region 2 . For a model this maps only as analogy: trained weights fit the skill side, but a skill file is read as text, which makes it closer to a declarative note. That mapping is inference; Milner 1962 was read only through Squire's account. Sources (2) Squire, The Legacy of Patient H.M. for Neuroscience ( opens in a new tab ) pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Squire, Conscious and Unconscious Memory Systems ( opens in a new tab ) pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov The agent changes the skill too, even on the same model in a benchmark of 98 public skills, 40 change sign between two harnesses running the same model, and the authors advise evaluating a skill "with the model, agent, and repositories in which it will be deployed" 1 . Sources (1) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Retire skills Retire a skill: archive over delete Knowledge-Centered Service prefers archiving to deleting, because deleting can break links and an archived article can be restored 1 . Anthropic says to deprecate a skill whose evaluations consistently fail or whose workflow is retired 2 . Reading the dive log to pick what to archive is the Episode's own method. Sources (2) Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, Technique 5.2: KCS Article State ( opens in a new tab ) library.serviceinnovation.org Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

The whole iceberg Skill governance: what is settled, and what is not no source defines owner and review date as a rule for skills, and none shows how many organisations govern shared skills at all 1 . The audience-by-scope matrix is a rule of thumb, not a published framework 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Saha and Hemanth, Skilldex: A Package Manager and Registry for Agent Skill Packages with Hierarchical Scope-Based Distribution ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

An AI model that forgets every morning 0:00 – 0:31 Three mornings So the next morning you open a new conversation, and the model knows nothing of yesterday. In our picture the pilot greets you with "Nice to meet you", you explain how to take the sediment sample step by step, and the robot waits on deck while you talk. The morning after, it is the same greeting and the same explanation, and by the third morning you could recite it in your sleep. 0:31 – 0:45 The hook That is what working with AI feels like today, because every conversation starts from zero on how you work. You've explained this to the AI a hundred times. It has heard it once. 0:45 – 1:09 What would you do So here is my question, and I would like your honest answer: if you worked with this model for a whole season, what would you do about it?
